body: The radio on the shelf above the parts bin has a strip of masking tape across the display, where the plastic cracked years ago. Half past three on a wet Friday, the shutter half down, two men in the garage: one under a car that has failed on emissions, the other at the bench doing very little and waiting to be handed something. A song comes on about a man who left, and who is not pretending he had a good reason, and who says so twice in the chorus. Neither of them speaks. The one at the bench reaches over and turns it up about two notches. Four minutes later, when the next song starts, he turns it back down and hands the other one the socket set.

Nobody in that garage would call it a religious experience, and it would be tactless to insist. But something was recognised and something was permitted, and the permission lasted exactly four minutes before the shutter came down on it again.

There is an odd inversion in what the two genres are willing to say out loud. Contemporary worship music has largely stopped singing about specific sin in the first person. There is a great deal of brokenness, which is vague and blameless, and rather less about a particular thing a particular person did on purpose.

The word doing the work in that sentence is brokenness, and it is a grammatical event as much as a theological one. Broken is a passive. Things get broken; nobody breaks himself. The word arrives with no agent attached and no object either — a person who is broken has not necessarily done anything to anyone, and cannot be asked what he did, because the condition happened to him. Compare the older vocabulary, which was aggressively first person and aggressively transitive. I did this. To her. On purpose. Twice. That grammar is not harsher for the sake of it; it is the only grammar in which forgiveness has anything to grip. You cannot be forgiven a passive construction. There is nobody in it to forgive.

Country music never gave that grammar up. It will sing, in the first person, about drink, adultery, walking out on children, prison, and the fact that the singer is not confident he is going to stop. On this band that lane sits in The Crossing, the block from HM 300 to HM 320, and there is a second country frequency assigned higher up which has not opened yet.

Programming that honestly is expensive in a way no invoice shows. A song that names damage and does not fix it by the last verse is hard to schedule, because it leaves the listener somewhere uncomfortable and the next track has to live with that. It is far easier to build a station where every three minutes resolves. The reason not to is simple. One of these traditions will sing about a man who has ruined his life and is not sure he will stop. The other one moved on from that some time ago, and what it moved on to is much easier to listen to and much harder to be told the truth by.

It is worth being fair about how the drift happened, because it was not cowardice. Worship music is congregational by design, and a congregational song has a hard constraint on it: a room full of people, of all ages and all histories, has to be able to sing it together without any one of them being made to confess something they have not done. Nobody can write a corporate chorus about a specific man leaving a specific woman in March. So the lyric abstracts, and it has to. The fault is not the abstraction. The fault is that the abstract song became the only kind most Christians hear, and a whole register went out of use because there was nowhere left to sing it.

You can see the same instinct in how the material is aimed. Modern worship is written to be sung by you, in the second person, upward: you are the voice, God is the addressee, the arrangement swells where the room is meant to lift. Country is written to be sung at you, sideways: somebody is telling you what he did, and you are not required to join in. The second arrangement is the older one and it does something the first cannot. It lets a person be present at a confession without having to make one.
That distinction is the whole argument, and it is not primarily about music.

The case for the worship chorus is genuinely strong and should not be waved away. Corporate praise is commanded, not optional, and a church that only sang first-person confession would be a miserable and self-absorbed place. Praise is meant to take a person out of himself, and the abstraction that makes a chorus singable by a room is the same abstraction that lets a widow and a teenager and a man with a criminal record sing one line at the same moment. All of that is real. What it cannot do — what it is structurally incapable of doing — is let one specific person say one specific true thing about himself out loud in a room.
A tradition that cannot name the damage cannot offer the forgiveness either.

A woman is driving her brother back from a hearing. It is about forty minutes and they have already done the talking they were going to do, which took eleven of them. He has his window down two inches in November because he says the heater is too much. On the radio a man is singing about having sold something that was not his to sell, and about his mother, and the song does not end with him putting any of it right. Her brother laughs once, not pleasantly, and says: that is about the size of it. She says nothing. Neither of them changes the station, and neither mentions it again that day or any day after, and she is still thinking about it four years later in a supermarket.

He said the one true sentence he was going to say that day, and he said it about a song rather than about himself. That is what the first-person confessional lyric does. It lends somebody a voice to stand behind while they tell the truth.

The honest cost is that country carries a great deal of other freight along with the honesty, and some of it is bad. The same tradition that will not flinch from naming a sin will, in the next song, sentimentalise it, romanticise the drink, make a virtue of the leaving, and mistake self-pity for penitence at length. A register that permits a man to say what he did also permits him to enjoy saying it. And an unresolved song is genuinely unresolved: it can leave a listener exactly where he was.

But an unresolved song is not a failure of nerve, and the scriptural precedent for it is usually skipped over. The penitential psalms are concrete, personal and occasionally not resolved at all. They are not about brokenness in general; they are about a man who did a thing and knows exactly what it was, and at least one of them ends in the dark with no comfort offered and is still in the book. That psalm was kept, and set to music, and sung for centuries, because somebody understood that a person in that condition needs a song that meets him there rather than one that hurries him out of it.

So the country lane on this band is not a stylistic concession to a region or a nod to anybody’s grandfather. It is carrying a register the rest of the catalogue is thin in — the one where a person can say what they actually did, out loud, without the song having to fix it by the end. The job is confession, and the steel-guitar accent is an accident of history rather than the point.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

There are two country frequencies on this dial. HM 373.80 Inspire Country sits up in The Living Room, and it is assigned, in build and not yet on air, so there is nothing playing there today; when it opens it will be the family-facing one, country as a room a household can sit in. The other is the one this article has been describing, and it is sounding now.

Start at HM 309.30, Gospel Country. I will be straight about why it is this one and not a fresher pick: it is the only frequency on the dial currently carrying this register, and an essay arguing that a particular honesty exists in exactly one place on the band would be dishonest to then send you somewhere else. Put it on in a car, or a workshop, or anywhere the volume can go up two notches without anybody asking why. Some of it will be too sentimental and some will resolve too neatly. Wait. Sooner or later a song arrives in which a man in the first person says the specific thing he did, and does not soften it, and does not tidy it away in the last verse — and you will find out quickly whether that register is one you have been missing, because the reaction to it is physical and it happens before you have decided anything.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download, no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built for inexpensive devices and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add the page to your home screen if you want it closer to hand. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

Take this as an invitation rather than a recommendation, because a recommendation implies you would be evaluating it. Put HM 309.30 on this weekend while you are doing something with your hands, and do not sit and listen attentively — that is not how this material has ever worked on anybody. Let it run. If a song comes on that you find yourself turning up two notches without deciding to, that is the register doing its job, and you can turn it back down four minutes later and hand somebody the socket set. Nothing further is required of you. That was always the point of a confession sung by somebody else.
